steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
### The Hack
- June 5, 2012: LinkedIn hacked, passwords for nearly 6.5 million accounts stolen by Russian cybercriminals
- owners locked out; site repeatedly told users to change passwords
- Vicente Silveira, director of LinkedIn, confirmed hack on official blog; compromised passwords no longer valid
- May 2016: additional 100 million email addresses + hashed passwords claimed to be from same 2012 breach
  - LinkedIn invalidated passwords of all users who had not changed them since 2012

### Leak
- data on more than 700 million users, believed scraped from LinkedIn
- leaked September 2021 as torrent file; hackers had tried to sell it in June 2021

### Reaction
- experts: passwords easy to unscramble because no salt when hashing; rainbow tables (pre-made lists of scrambled/unscrambled passwords)
- iOS app controversy: grabs names, emails, notes from mobile calendar without approval
  - Skycure Security experts: app sends personal data to LinkedIn server
  - LinkedIn: permission user-granted, sent securely over SSL; never stored or shared with third party
- Congress
  - Rep. Mary Bono Mack: [quote: "How many times..." / need for data protection legislation]
  - Senator Patrick Leahy: [quote: give pause to American consumers / data privacy and cybercrime legislation top priority]
- Marcus Carey (Rapid7): hackers in LinkedIn databases in preceding days; may have had access even after attack
- Michael Aronowitz (VP, Saveology): [quote: hundreds of sites hacked every day, login reuse]
- experts: passwords encrypted in a way fairly easy to decrypt, one reason for breach
- Lawsuit
  - Katie Szpyrka, long-time user from Illinois: $5 million lawsuit, promises on secure connections and databases not kept
  - spokeswoman Erin O’Harra: lawyers taking advantage to again propose SOPA and PIPA
  - amended complaint Nov. 26, 2012: Szpyrka + Khalilah Gilmore–Wright (premium user, Virginia) as class representatives
  - sought injunctive and other equitable relief, restitution and damages

### Response from LinkedIn
- apologized immediately, asked users to change passwords
- FBI assisted the investigation
- as of 8 June 2012 investigation early; couldn't tell if email addresses also stolen
- users with compromised passwords could not log in with old passwords

### The Hack

On June 5, 2012, the social networking website LinkedIn was hacked, and Russian cybercriminals stole the passwords for nearly 6.5 million user accounts. The owners of the hacked accounts could no longer access their accounts, and after the incident the website kept encouraging its users to change their passwords. Vicente Silveira, who was the director of LinkedIn, confirmed for the company in its official blog that the website was hacked. He also said that holders of the compromised accounts would find that their passwords were not valid on the website anymore.

In May 2016, LinkedIn found an additional 100 million email addresses and hashed passwords which were claimed to be more data from the same 2012 breach. LinkedIn responded by invalidating the passwords of all users who had not changed their password since 2012.

### Leak

In September, 2021 a collection with data about more than 700 million users, which is believed to have been scraped from LinkedIn, was leaked online as a torrent file, after hackers had already tried to sell it earlier, in June, 2021.

### Reaction

- no salt when hashing -> easy to unscramble with standard rainbow tables (pre-made lists of matching scrambled and unscrambled passwords)
- iOS app grabs names, emails, notes from calendar without approval; Skycure Security: sends data to LinkedIn server; LinkedIn: user-granted, sent over SSL, never stored or shared with third party
- Congress: Rep. Mary Bono Mack quote ("How many times is this going to happen before Congress finally wakes up and takes action? ..."); Senator Patrick Leahy quote ("Reports of another major data breach should give pause to American consumers ...")
- Marcus Carey (Rapid7): hackers in databases in preceding days, maybe access after attack
- Michael Aronowitz (Saveology) quote ("Everyday hundreds of sites are hacked ..."); experts: passwords fairly easy to decrypt
- Katie Szpyrka (Illinois) $5 million lawsuit; Erin O’Harra: lawyers using it to again propose SOPA and PIPA
- amended complaint Nov. 26, 2012, with Khalilah Gilmore–Wright (Virginia), class representatives; injunctive and equitable relief, restitution, damages

### Response from LinkedIn

- apologized immediately, asked users to change passwords
- FBI assisted; 8 June 2012 still early, unclear if email addresses stolen
- compromised users can't log in with old passwords

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
### The Hack

On June 5, 2012, the social networking website LinkedIn was hacked, and Russian cybercriminals stole the passwords for nearly 6.5 million user accounts. The owners of the hacked accounts could no longer access their accounts, and after the incident the website kept encouraging its users to change their passwords. Vicente Silveira, who was the director of LinkedIn, confirmed for the company in its official blog that the website was hacked. He also said that holders of the compromised accounts would find that their passwords were not valid on the website anymore.

In May 2016, LinkedIn found an additional 100 million email addresses and hashed passwords which were claimed to be more data from the same 2012 breach. LinkedIn responded by invalidating the passwords of all users who had not changed their password since 2012.

### Leak

In September, 2021 a collection with data about more than 700 million users, which is believed to have been scraped from LinkedIn, was leaked online as a torrent file, after hackers had already tried to sell it earlier, in June, 2021.

### Reaction

Internet security experts said the passwords were easy to unscramble because LinkedIn did not use a salt when it hashed them. This is considered an insecure practice because attackers can quickly reverse the scrambling using existing standard rainbow tables, which are pre-made lists of matching scrambled and unscrambled passwords. Another thing that caused controversy was LinkedIn's iOS app, which grabs personal names, emails, and notes from a mobile calendar without the user approving it. Security experts who worked for Skycure Security said that the app collects a user's personal data and sends it to the LinkedIn server. LinkedIn said that the permission for this feature is granted by the user, and that the information is sent securely using the Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) protocol. The company also said it had never stored the information or shared it with a third party.

Rep. Mary Bono Mack of the United States Congress commented on the incident, "How many times is this going to happen before Congress finally wakes up and takes action? This latest incident once again brings into sharp focus the need to pass data protection legislation." Senator Patrick Leahy said, "Reports of another major data breach should give pause to American consumers who, now more than ever, share sensitive personal information in their online transactions and networking ... Congress should make comprehensive data privacy and cybercrime legislation a top priority."

Marcus Carey, who is a security researcher for Rapid7, said that the hackers had gotten into the databases of LinkedIn in the days before. He was concerned that they might have had access to the website even after the attack.

Michael Aronowitz, Vice President of Saveology, said, "Everyday hundreds of sites are hacked and personal information is obtained. Stealing login information from one account can easily be used to access other accounts, which can hold personal and financial information." Security experts said that the stolen passwords had been encrypted in a way that was fairly easy to decrypt, and this was one of the reasons for the data breach.

Katie Szpyrka, who had used LinkedIn for a long time and is from Illinois, United States, filed a $5 million lawsuit against LinkedIn. She complained that the company had not kept its promises to secure connections and databases. When Erin O’Harra, a spokeswoman for LinkedIn, was asked about the lawsuit, she said that lawyers were looking to take advantage of the situation to propose the bills SOPA and PIPA in the United States Congress again.

On Nov. 26, 2012 an amended complaint was filed on behalf of Szpyrka and another premium LinkedIn user, Khalilah Gilmore–Wright from Virginia, United States, as class representatives for all LinkedIn users affected by the breach. The lawsuit asked for injunctive and other equitable relief, and also restitution and damages for the plaintiffs and the members of the class.

### Response from LinkedIn

Right after the data breach LinkedIn apologized and asked its users to change their passwords immediately. The Federal Bureau of Investigation helped the LinkedIn Corporation investigate the theft. As of 8 June 2012 the investigation was still in its early stages, and the company said it could not determine whether the hackers had also been able to steal the email addresses that went with the compromised user accounts. LinkedIn said that users whose passwords were compromised would not be able to access their LinkedIn accounts with their old passwords.
